do so. If I give the amount' expended, of course hon. members will have the amount on hand, to which my chief of staff objects.

That would be assuming we would be making no ammunition here in Canada. I do not ask as to the exact amount of ammunition on hand all told, but it would seem to me that we might, in view of what has transpired in the past, have some information as to what portion of the ammunition that came from England since the war is still on hand, and I certainly did want to know, with as much certainty as possible, what portion, if any, will not be useful. The minister said it would all be useful, except any portion that may not be used up to the time at which it is not supposed to be useful, which I think is 1925. Could the minister not tell us, assuming the consumption continues at the existing rate, whether or not all that munition will be used before it becomes useless in July 1925?
At the present rate of consumption of ammunition, it will not all be used before 1925.
Will the minister g6 just a little further and give us some idea of the quantity? Is the quantity to be on hand trifling?
It will be trifling.
That is satisfactory.

The minister says that the heads of his department do not want him to tell how much ammunition there is in stock. I would remind the minister that last year he gave us that information. He evidently did not at that time follow the advice of his military advisers. This year, when we require similar information, we cannot get it because his military advisers tell him that he should not give it.

I know quite well I gave figures last year, and that is the reason why I was warned by my Chief of Staff that I did a wrong thing. last year. I was asked on the floor of the House to give certain figures and I gave them as nearly as possible. When this year I asked my Chief of Staff what I should do, he said that I should, if possible, refrain in the meantime from giving the quantity of ammunition on hand.

As a consequence, the minister is not prepared to state how much small arms ammunition was used at the camps this year. The last time these estimates were up I asked whether it was necessary to continue manufacturing these goods. That can be determined only by knowing how much we have
on hand. We are running an ammunition factory at considerable expense, and if we have on hand enough ammunition for a period of years with a reduced military camp, the best thing to do is to give the ammunition factory a rest for a while.

The approximate quantity of small arms ammunition used last year was
4,000,000 rounds. As regards the other question, there is a limit of reserve under which Canada has gone. I will go that far. She will be manufacturing for some little time before she arrives at the place at which she ought to arrive and make provision for the annual expenditure.

I am glad to know that we used about 4,000,000 rounds of small arm3 ammunition. Last year, the minister told us that assuming that we were using about nine or ten million rounds a year we required of small arms ammunition enough for about a five years' supply. That would be about 45,000,000 rounds. Now, he tells us that the amount we used last year was 4,000,000 rounds. According to those statements, we have enough small arms ammunition to do us for ten years, assuming that we shall not use it at a higher rate than we did last year, and from the militia estimates that we are passing, we cannot use more because we are reducing the camps. This ammunition will spoil if we keep it without using it for ten years, and as far as I can see we have enough on hand now to last us for ten years. What is the use of making more?

I tried to explain to my hon. friend a point that has some delicacy to it. We are supposed to have on hand in Canada at all times a certain number of rounds of ammunition for safety. We have not that nor anything approaching it, and if what my hon. friend said were true, that would not help the situation in the least degree, because if we are to approximate the number of rounds we ought to have in the Dominion of Canada, we must manufacture all we use and a great deal more.
What is the life of small arms ammunition? How many years is it supposed to be good for?
About ten years.
After that, provided there is any of it on hand, what is done with it?

It is tested at certain times. Of course, one can understand that ammunition that was dangerous could not be used for any remanufacturing purposes. It is generally destroyed.

No such suggestion as that has been made to me. I am inclined, however, to think if we were thrown immediately into the midst of war with a high or peak expenditure of explosives, we would not have enough to last very long.

not advise that we had just one day's supply in such an emergency as that?

I have been endeavouring to gather from the minister's statements what is the government's policy with regard to national defence. I understand from the minister that the supply of ammunition on hand is very much below the estimated reserve necessary to ensure the safety of the country. The arsenal at Lindsay has been closed, but there is an increase in the vote for the Quebec arsenal. The naval service has been sent on a fishing expedition. The colleges for training cadets for the naval eer-

vice at Esquimalt and Halifax have been closed. Does the minister consider that any useful purpose is being served by the vote now under consideration for national defence or for the training of what is left of our militia? I must say that. I am unable to understand from the explanations which have been given what the ultimate object of the government is. Some time ago the people were led to believe that certain hon. gentlemen opposite were horrified to think that large quantities of ammunition were being brought to Quebec from Great Britain. Now we are told by the minister that the supply is largely below the quantity required for the national safety in the event of any trouble arising. Is it prudent or advisable to get below the safety line in connection with national defence? Surely the dignity of the country and our national selfrespect must be maintained, and these can only be maintained by keeping our reserve of ammunition at a point which will enable us to take care of ourselves in the event of any emergency.

It is hard work to divide my affections in this matter. An hon. gentleman (Mr. Chaplin) near my friend from Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) chastised me a moment ago for making more ammunition while we have some on hand; my friend from Oxford says that we are not going fast enough in building up a reserve. The purpose of this vote is the manufacture of ammunition. I agree with him that as rapidly as possible we ought to approximate at least to what our officers in charge of national defence think is the proper reserve.

It is quite evident
from the minister's reply that the officers of the department did not report that the ammunition which was unloaded at Quebec a couple of years ago was any menace to this country as then intimated by hon. gentlemen opposite.

I did not hear the first part of my hon. friend's remarks about the

Supply-Defence
Vickers case. Will he tell me what he refers to as the basis of the Vickers case? What is the ground of their claim?
The basis was damages for the cancellation of a contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the crux of the whole matter. The whole matter hinges on that word " cancellation There was no cancellation; that is the vital point of the whole thing. In the discussion which took place a year ago my hon. friend made a similar remark; he understood there had been a cancellation of a contract, and therefore there would have to be compensation paid in soma form under it. It may be that there are facts in this matter which did not come before me. The settlement of the claim was not part of my mission to England, but while there I had an opportunity of making some inquiries into the matter and had the privilege of hearing the views of Sir Trevor Dawson, managing director of the Vickers Company. As I found the case there was no cancellation at all. The Vickers Company made a contract with the government of Canada. The government of Canada were ready to honour the contract; they were ready to take the goods and pay for them. But the Vickers Company did not deliver the goods; they could not deliver them. The war came on, the British government took possession of the Vickers concern, and the Vickers people were busy from that time forward in fulfilling contracts with the British government. There was no cancellation on the part of the Dominion of Canada. That is the vital thing. If I am right in that then the Vickers Company have no claim. I have to emphasize that fact as matters all depend on that. It was said the claim was admitted later on. Even if that were so it would not be fatal at all; much would depend on the party who had admitted it and his authority to make the admission. But there was no such admission. An officer representing my hon. friend, who was then Minister of Militia, stated to the Vickers that if there were to be any further orders given, all things feeing equal, a preference would be given to the Vickers over other parties. But no further orders were given about that time, and there came no opportunity for the granting of the preference which was indicated. But if I am right in my statement the whole thing turns upon the question: Was there a cancellation of the contract? My information is that there was not. The government made a contract, the government were ready to receive the goods, the government were ready to pay for them, but the Vickers never could deliver the goods. The contract contained a clause respecting penalty and technically speak-111
ing there might be a claim for damages. But that would not be urged under the circumstances. The Vickers Company were not able to deliver the goods because the British government took possession of their works. I think there would be great difficulty in saying that the Vickers Company made any large expenditure bearing on the contract. If they made any expenditure it would be a very small one. If they did incur any expenditure designed to serve the contract, I suppose we might say technically there was a claim against the British government, because it was something the British govermnent did, and not anything the Canadian government did, that prevented the carrying out of the contract. If the claim were made that the Vickers Company had expended some money in preparing for the contract, to that small extent there might be a fair claim; but any claim based on the contention that there was a cancellation of the contract is, if my own information is correct, entirely unfounded. I want to say that in this vote for the air force $250,000 is for the purchase of equipment, flying machines, etc. This service is going to be more useful year by year, as hon. gentlemen will see if they look into what has been done during the past year. I may as well tell the committee that this service is not going to be an inexpensive one. Machines last but a very short time and wear out quickly; the spare parts that have to be carried are expensive; the whole service is quite a costly one. But in one year it more than repays what it will cost in ten in the preservation of our forests and other preventive measures. This $250,000 will include the purchase of nine amphibious machines; in other words, flying boats. They will cost in the vicinity of $175,000. Tenders were accepted-they have not been delivered yet-from the Vickers people, seven of these to be manufactured in the Dominion of Canada and two to be manufactured in Great Britain and sent over. The wireless, for. which an appropriation is asked in the $250,000, is one of the branches of aerial service. Without the ability to communicate with their headquarters on the ground, flying over the forest is somewhat precarious and not practicable. In addition to that, in the city of Winnipeg, for the purchase of some land, on which an amount has been spent this year in the erection of hangars, I think in the vicinity of about $1,000 will be expended, and the balance of this is for operation and maintenance, etc. I might say that last year some difficulty was found, I think particularly in the province of Quebec, with some of the large machines. When they got into difficulty and alighted on some of the small lakes, it was almost impossible to get them out. They were unsuitable for that work. These machines were practically all given to us by the Royal Air Force of the British government, and of necessity a good many of them have got to the point where they are unsafe for use and others are of a nature and construction not quite practicable in this country. In another year we will have to buy more machines for two reasons, first, because the machines are constantly wearing out, and, second, because men must not be sent in the air in machines that are considered unsafe. Furthermore, the de-
[Mr. Graham.3
mands being made on the air force are doubled every year. Last year the Attorney General of British Columbia came in to see me, and asked if we could not extend the service in British Columbia. He pointed out two or three instances in connection with the work out there that would impress one with the value of the service being rendered by the air force. He is Minister of Lands, and in one instance there was a point which he, with those in his department wished to reach. He told me it would have taken him several days, I forget how many, by pack train to get to this point. He went in with one of our machines and made the inspection, and only three hours were occupied in getting there. In expense, feed and practicability the air service has overcome time and distance.
Last year we received from the province of Quebec $20,000, and the same amount from the province of Ontario. Ontario has paid us $38,000 this year, having increased its service. British Columbia paid us a certain amount but the attorney general told me they were prepared to pay $20,000 this year and were prepared to extend and enlarge this service.
Has this service been extended to Saskatchewan? If so how much was spent there last year?

The province of Saskatchewan is looked after largely from the Winnipeg depot. There has not been any work done, except some observation work, as far as I can recollect, in the province of Saskatchewan. We cannot very well locate these provincial activities, and distance does not mean much, if anything, to a flying machine, and for the present at least the officers of the department are confident that with the improvements they intend to make at Winnipeg, all the needs of Saskatchewan can be amply taken care of for some years to come.

Has provision been
made for the province of New Brunswick and the province of Quebec?

I think we have not been successful in entering into any arrangement with the province of New Brunswick as yet, although we have a station in Nova Scotia from which they can do work in the province of New Brunswick and Quebec.

Some weeks ago we had a debate in this House with regard to the building of the Hudson Bay railway. Has the minister given any consideration to the feasibility of using the air force for the purpose of investigating the Hudson bay route and

Supply-Defence
of determining the exact time in each year that that route Would be open to navigation?

I think it has been decided already by the department that a portion of the air force shall visit Nelson and Churchill during the summer. An attempt is being made now to have an excursion trip by boat up to Nelson. A member of the air force proposes to accompany that party, if it materializes.

That only applies to a certain season of the year. What I meant was a prolonged investigation over the whole period of one year, say, so that we could ascertain the nature of the channels and the route during the fall and winter months, and spring as well.

Up to date we have not had sufficient money to enlarge to that extent. I might say that the Northwest branch has been urging us to establish a post much further north, but we have no money in this estimate for that purpose.

Does the minister not consider that it would be advisable to postpone further expenditure on the Hudson Bay railway until such an investigation could be carried out, it being about the only means we have in our power of carrying out a thorough investigation as to the feasibility of that loute?
My hon. friend from the other angle here would not agree to take that as a reason for postponing any work on the Hudson Bay railway.
Not after the promise of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell).

Which seems to have been ineffective. Consequently I do not feel like making any more promises. A good many miles of the Hudson Bay railway, of course, have been constructed and investigations have been made. Everyone who has a library has volumes replete with investigations of the Hudson Bay railway, and I think we have got beyond the point when we can say that the Hudson Bay railway cannot be constructed unless we can further convince ourselves of its necessity.

In connection with .this item, is any provision made for the improvement of the approaches to this camp? The camp is in my riding, I am very familiar with it, and I certainly approve of this item. I think that in the interest of heavy trucks which
llli
operate there something should be done. The camp is reached from Angus on the Grand Trunk, and on the south from Alliston. There is about a mile of road within the camp from the Angus end which is simply a disgrace. It is not a road at all. It is a sand trail winding all over, the trucks get . stuck, and I have no doubt considerable damage is done to the trucks from time to time. Within the camp itself, I do not know how many miles, but from 6 to 10 miles of cement pavement have been constructed during the activities of the camp in the years 1915	and 1916.
Tt seems a pity that those stationed at. the camp and many citizens of Canada who have occasion, from time to time, to visit the camp, should have to use the bit of road to which I refer. The work would not cost very much. I think the matter has been brought to the attention of the minister by some of the residents of Angus, and I feel satisfied that the municipalities interested would take care of the very small portion leading from Angus to the entrance to the camp, if the department would devote simply a reasonable amount of money to improve the road from the entrance to the camp to connect with the cement pavement now there. I am sure if the minister saw the place, nothing further would be necessary to convince him that the work should be undertaken mainly in connection with the heavy loads that go in and out of that camp. If there is nothing in the item now for this work, I would express the hope that the minister might economize on some of the other items making up the total and take this work in hand. If any other evidence is necessary respecting the need of this road improvement, I would be glad to busy myself and to supply the minister with it. I remember a gentleman coming down from Angus and interviewing the minister. He presented the matter very forcibly; but so far as I know, nothing has been done since. 1 hope the minister will give this matter his consideration.

We will certainly give it consideration. It has been brought to my attention by the hon. gentleman before and by a gentleman in that vicinity. I had hoped to be at Camp Borden last summer with my hon. friend, and if we could not travel over the road any other way, we would fly over it.
I understood the minister to say that several of the provinces had contributed S20,000 to the military air force, is that right?

Yes.
Supply-Defence
Does the air force do any flying for private concerns?

We have a receipt for $733 for urgent work done during a fire. I imagine that if there was any commercial work to be done, the air force would not be above handling it, if it did not interfere with their other, work. At the present time we have not a' sufficiently large vote to go into that; but I think it has been the general consensus of opinion that commercial flying for purposes of gain should be left largely to private enterprise rather than that it should be undertaken by the government.	.

I would like to revert to a matter I brought to the attention of the minister a few moments ago. I have been advised by people who, I consider, are experts in this service, that it would be possible, to carry on such an investigation as I suggested. In the debate on the Hudson Bay railway, considerable doubt seems to exist as to the exact period of time that the Hudson bay is open to navigation. I have also been informed by an authority that appears to be fairly good that there is a possibility that Hudson bay is open for navigation for a much longer period of time than was suggested by the mover of the resolution the other day; that furthermore, we could prove or disprove that by an investigation carried out by the air force, and that if such an investigation was properly planned over a full period of one year, we could determine almost to a final degree the exact period of time that that bay would be open to navigation during a year. I seriously commend this to the attention of the minister in the hope that in the very near future our air force can be used for the purpose of carrying out such an investigation. It seems to be perfectly futile to send an expedition up there in the summer time to gather such information.

I might say, as the mover of the resolution, that I took the reports of a number of investigations which had been made covering a number of years, because conditions in Hudson bay and in the strait are not always the same, and it is necessary to take a number of years before one can reach a proper conclusion. I really believe an investigation such as has been suggested might do a great deal of good. It has been suggested that investigations should be made by the air force up in the Fox channel to discover the sources of the field ice which comes down in the spring and fall. It is possible we might learn a great deal regarding that by

an expedition of that kind. I do not think, however, an expedition into Hudson bay or strait for one season would determine anything more than what we know at the present time. I took it as conclusive that the investigation which had been made by the Senate committee at that time and which was brought down in their report, covered the matter as far as we could get at it just now.

Is it the policy of the government at the present time in the air force to have the machines all shipped to one central point to be repaired? If so, does the minister think that is the best way of handling repairs to these machines?

We have now three central shops in which they could be repaired, and it is questionable whether it would pay to establish shops with all their equipment at any more points for the limited number of machines we have. This is not like anything else. When a machine needs some repairs, but is not altogether out of repair, it can go in a very few minutes quite a long distance to a shop, and it can return at the same speed.
Where are those three central repair shops?

High River, Ottawa and
Camp Borden. There is a small shop at Vancouver. There are two or three other small shops besides the one I mentioned.

When I was coming down
to this session of parliament, there were five airmen on the train who were being shipped from Vancouver to Camp Borden to engage in repair work. Very shortly after the session opened, I received a letter from those men. I think it is in the interest of this House that we should know these facts, and if there is any truth in them, I feel sure the minister Whuld be glad to look into the matter. This letter is dated Camp Borden, February 5, and it goes on to say:
I learn that militia estimates are now before the House, so am taking this privilege of offering more facts to bear out our claims as to the waste of public funds under military control.
The letter refers to the Air Board. That has now been changed to the air force. It continues :
There are men here sent from every Air Board station, including High River, Winnipeg, Roberval and Quebec, to do work on engines and wings that are shipped from above stations and which will be reshipped on completion. Outside of this waste in men's time, travelling, fares and freight on engines and wings, we can truthfully say after being here ten days, that the amount of work done here is about 30 per cent of what we do at our own stations.

Supply-Defence
One instance of waste came before us to-day in so much that a man examined by a military doctor in Vancouver was shipped to this camp, examined by the military doctor here and proclaimed medically unlit.
At Vancouver air station men are being drilled three hours a day and three days a week. At the above station we have one serviceable machine, yet with seven men away doing duty here, the remainder are forced to waste their time forming fours and saluting, stuff that we all got during the war and quite unnecessary.
The men that have been relied upon this last three years are Air Board men, men that got their knowledge during the war and have trades behind them and which are an asset to Canada and aviation. These men are now wasting their time here, owing to a poor organization and military red tape.
I have gone amongst these men and in fact working with them right now and can safely say that not more than two per cent would join a permanent force. It's quite evident as to the class of men that would go to make up Canada's air force, should one be formed, just men that are out for an easy time and men unable to do so well outside.
Another instance of military inefficiency, a man here was made sergeant who has to get a second-class mechanic to do his work, being quite incapable to handle tools himself at all. I could go on relating instances of waste and inefficiency and am confident that any money voted to the military cause will be an absolute waste of public funds.
The men that know this business and are behind this letter, and have made a name in commercial aviation will have nothing to do with such a cause, so where the military party have an argument at all I fail to see.
I hope the minister will look into this matter and ascertain whether or not these charges of militar}' inefficiency are substantiated by the facts.

I do not know who signs
that letter, but whoever he is, he is a first-class grouch. I will not ask for his name.

I do not care to give his
name.

No, I do not want it,
but I shall have the contents of the letter looked into. I feel confident that they are not borne out by the facts. At all events I shall have the matter investigated.
I thank the minister.

Could the minister go
on with some other items instead of this? We should like to have this stand over for a day, and we could proceed with others. We have no intention of holding up the estimates at all.
This winds up my Defence estimates, except for the supplementaries.
Is this the only item?
There are two items which we are discussing together.
So far as I am concerned I have no objection to one of the items going through, but I would ask that this one be allowed to stand.
Very well.
At what distance can these machines operate from the base of supply?
It depends on the size of the machine I should say, 200 or 250 miles.

In that case I would point out that, an air force with a base at lake Winnipeg could not operate in northern Saskatchewan. We have immense areas of forest there that should be protected and an up-to-date system is absolutely necessary. Seeing that the forests in Saskatchewan are the property of the federal government, I think it is only fair that a station should be established in some part of northern Saskatchewan where the work could be looked after better.

There has been an urgent appeal for the establishment of a station at Cowan lake, but we shall have to ask for a larger estimate if we are to set up more flying station establishments. At present there are orders from the various provinces for more work than the department can supply machines or men to cover, and it is a question whether we shall not have to enlarge the scope of the air force both as to men and machines.

speechtext: Shall item 114 carry? Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Item 115 stands.
National Defence-amount required to pay cost of living bonus to employees of the Dominion arsenal and others at Quebec, discharged without receiving bonus for certain periods for which it was later granted to those similarly employed and not discharged, $26,000.

In 1920 the Quebec arsenal was closed for a short period, and at that time it had not yet been decided whether these men were entitled to the bonus. In the interval, however, it was held by the Civil Service Commission that the bonus was due. Those men who were taken on again and who returned to work were given the bonus, but those who did not resume work did not get it, although the bonus was earned before the closing of the arsenal. It is maintained, I think in perfect honesty, that the men were all equally entitled to the bonus once the commission had held that it was properly payable.

If I remember the facts rightly, during the year 1921 both the arsenal at Lindsay and the arsenal at Quebec were closed for two or three months and the staffs were also considerably reduced. I was not aware that a bonus was at all payable to these men. Has it been subsequently decided that

Supply-RaUimys
those who were retained were entitled to it? As I understand, they were men working for wages at so much per day; they were mechanics and the like who were laid off. Was there any bonus applicable to them?

I would not express an opinion on that. In 1920-it was not 1921- the bonus was paid to the men who were taken back after the arsenal was re-opened. It was paid on the decision of the department and the Civil Service Commission. The men who were not taken on did not get it although they had earned the bonus equally with the others. They now claim it and the commission' decides that they are entitled to it.

I do not understand it yet. Were the men wage-earners or salaried, and if they were wage-earners, did they not follow the regular scale of advance given at that time in lieu of bonus? I do not claim to have a distinct recollection of the matter at all, but it would occur to me that this means two bonuses. Does it apply to both arsenals?

I am informed that although the men were working by the day it was decided they were entitled to the bonus and they got it in 1920. The Deparment of Labour, I believe, took a hand in the matter, and it was finally decided and approved by the Civil Service Commission that these men were entitled to the bonus. The men who were taken on again got the cash. The men who. were not taken on again were entitled under the decision just the same as the men who did come on after the reopening of the arsenal.
These men were not taken back?
Yes; but the bonus was earned before the arsenal was closed, and it was paid to the men for the period prior to the closing.
I do not remember the matter ever coming up in the time of the late government.
It was in 1920.

It may have been advanced, but I do not think it was. Were there not advances made in lieu of bonus to the same men? And would there not be quite a number of these men now dead? I do not know how you are going to pay the bonuses three years afterwards.

I am not familiar with the situation but I do know it was in 1920. After the arsenal reopened the men that
[Mr. Guthrie.)
were taken on were paid the bonus for a time prior to the closing of the arsenal. This vote is to pay the men who were not taken back.

I would not have the least sympathy with any neglect to pay extra wages to wage-earners commensurate, or even more than commensurate, with the bonus as extra remuneration to salaried employees. The minister says that this is merely the pro rata allowance based on time of service of the men who had to be laid off commensurate with that secured by those who did not have to be laid off, or who being laid off were taken back. Does it apply to the men employed in both arsenals?
I am told it did not apply to the Lindsay arsenal. For what reason I do not know.
It is just possible, of course, that none were released until just lately. But I think we should have the reasor before we pass the vote..

I have no objection to letting the item stand. The situation I believe is quite clear. Certain men who claimed the bonus were working at the Quebec arsenal. Before the arsenal closed it had not been decided that they were entitled to the bonus. After the reopening it was decided and approved by the Civil Service Commission that these men who had claimed .the bonus prior to the closing were entitled to it. Those who came back got it under the decision: those who did not come back, did not get it.
Before the item comes up again perhaps the minister will bring down the report of the Civil Service Commission on the subject so we will see the argument by which they arrived at their decision.
For what period was this bonus paid?

From the 1st April to the 1st August 1920.
Item stands.
