speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The explanation of this item is that when the estimates were voted for the railway service it was contemplated that these sums, amounting to about $13,000,000, in the form of obligations coming due might be renewed, in which case it would not be necessary to provide for them in this way. When the obliga-

Supply-Railways
tions became due it was found convenient for the moment to pay them out of the general treasury, and it became necessary to vote this amount to cover the payment. It is still possible they may be consolidated, but in the meantime it is necessary to make the appropriation because the payment that was made was not contemplated when the estimate was voted.

In connection with the
general subject, it would seem to me that in case of a renewal of this sort the item shoul '* be in the estimates anyway so that each year we could easily see just how much of the money and of the credit of the country was advanced for deficits or for capital expenditure to the railways. Supposing it were a fact that this was a maturing obligation, and it was expected to renew the obligation, in that event, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has stated there would be no need of making the amount of the renewal appear in the estimates at all. On the other hand, suppose it had been intended that that obligation would be paid off by the issue of a new security guaranteed by the government. Then, as I understand the system that has always been followed, that new undertaking of the government would appear included in the estimates voted for the year. Well, had there been an intended renewal it would be a renewal with a government obligation. Consequently it seems to me it should have been included anyway.
I think I have a correct idea as to the facts and I hope I have made myself clear. I would like to have the minister's version of the situation. Is it not a fact that the estimates are supposed to include all the moneys advanced and as well all the obligations to be incurred direct or indirect by,the country for the fiscal year in respect of the railways? If so, would it not have been right to have had this included anyway if it was the intention of the government to guarantee the obligation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is something to be said for my right hon. friend's contention that these maturing obligations might be shown in the estimates. I think, however, that that has not been the practice. Where an appropriation is made it is an appropriation in anticipation to meet a deficiency and not to include renewals. I think there is something to be said in favour of showing renewals but I am quite safe in saying that it has not been the practice in the past. New securities have been issued to make way for old ones, but I do not think they are shown in the estimates. I am not sure that there is not something in the contention of my right hon. friend, and that matter may be considered when preparing the estimates in the future.

I have been somewhat bothered by that complication of the entire railway financial situation. I do not know whether it has been conducted in exactly the right way in the past or not, but I do urge that we ought to have a system by which the estimates will include all obligations, whether by way of cash advances or guarantees for the ensuing year by the country with respect to the railways. I am sure I am right. If I had the former Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) I might get along by asking him instead of bringing it up in this way. Is it not a fact that the minister's estimates for the year include not only cash that is *going to be required from the Treasury by way of loan-for everything is by way of loan as I understand it-whether for capital investment, extensions of lines or for deficit? All the money that is advanced is included in the estimate for the roads, and as well, all the obligations intended to be entered into by way of guarantee-for I know the estimate reads in such a way as to enable the minister to do it by way of guarantee. Is it not a fact that the minister's estimates for this year include all those obligations to be incurred in respect of the railways, whether by cash advance or by guarantee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the estimates are for what I may call the current expenditures of the year. The wording of the estimate very properly allows the government to make payment either by way of cash or by bonds or by guarantees-in any form it pleases. But I do not think it covers renewals-that is my impression. I am inclined to the view, however, that we might well show the nature of these maturing obligations from time to time; and that thought may well engage our consideration hereafter.

I think I have the point now: The intention of the estimates, as the minister understands it, has been to include all moneys to be advanced to the roads, and, as well, all obligations, whether by guarantee or otherwise-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not renewals.
-whether by guarantee or otherwise that go to increase the debt of the railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To meet the obligations of the railway for the current year.

and the government decided that that should be done by the issue of a bond of the railway company which would have to be guaranteed by the government, then the estimates would include that; but if it were merely for renewal of a past obligation, in no way extending the debt of the system, the estimates would not include it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

I quite agree that it would be better for the estimates only to provide, as in the past, for all moneys to be advanced and all guarantees to be included that go to increase the railway's obligations. Those should be separate, but I think the others should appear, in a different place-all that increases the government's obligations, even for renewals. I am afraid I am not making myself very clear. I think it is right-and I am pretty sure this is what has been found in the past by both governments-that the estimates should show distinctly the entire commitments intended by the country for the railways in so far as those commitments increase the obligations of the system; all the others should be separate in the future as in the past. But I think the estimates
5 p.m. should include as well any further obligations the country enters into on behalf of the railways for renewals, because those increase the country's obligations. It would never do, though, to have these included in the estimates in the same body as the rest; if we did that it would present the obligations of the country in too big a form, because while we are increasing the national obligations we are diminishing the obligations of the company that we own. It would never do to include the one with the other; I think they both should be there, but separate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My understanding is that the appropriation each year involves what I may again describe as the current expenditure of the year-not, however, on what might be called capital account. If, for example, a branch line is constructed, I think it would be necessary for the minister to bring in a special appropriation act for the purpose; I do not think we would have an appropriation to cover that. I may say, for example, certain appro- [DOT] priations will be needed in the way of equipment bonds. The railway legislation gives the railway company the power to issue these bonds; no appropriation here will be required. As a matter of convenience it might be well to show in the estimate of each year the maturing obligations. But it is necessary to draw a line between what I might call the current expenditure of the year and obliga-
TMr. Meighen.]
tions which are represented by outstanding securities which can be renewed, as was the case in this matter. This may later be converted into securities, but in the meantime, as it was paid out of the. current appropriation, we have to have this supplementary estimate to make it good. The suggestion that these maturing obligations, even in the way of renewals, should be shown in the estimate, is worthy of consideration, and without making any absolute engagement in the matter, I would like to see it considered hereafter.
May I ask the Minister of Railways whether there is to be any revision of the boundaries of the eastern region?

That is a matter that
rests with the Canadian National Railways Board. It is not part of the government's duty to dictate to the board as to how they shall operate and what areas shall constitute the different regions. That is purely an operative question.

I appreciate the difficulty
of the position in which the minister finds himself and in which any minister dealing with this department must find himself in regard to a question of this kind. It is put forward very definitely that this railroad is to be kept out of politics. One might hope that that may be so. I have heard gentlemen in the presence of Sir Henry Thornton declare, however, that it is impossible to keep the railroad out of politics. I do not know just what particular political interference they had in mind, though I have my suspicions. But there is a certain class of politics out of which no government can keep a state-owned railway. The government must lay down a policy for the railroad, which is a very different thing from allowing henchmen to dictate who shall be appointees to particular minor positions. As to the latter, I think we all concur that the railroad should be kept out of politics, but as to necessary action to ensure that all parts of the country through which the railroad runs shall have fair and just treatment and shall receive the co-operation of the national road in the matter of realizing their aspirations as well as meeting their needs *-so far as that is concerned, the railroad neither should be nor will be kept out of politics.
We, in the Maritime provinces do not, I trust, complain unduly, but we do come here with a desire to let our needs be known, and if we feel that we are not getting in any respect the treatment that we ought to have, this parliament is the place in which we

Supply-Railways
should express our views in that respect. It is quite proper that boards of trade in the Maritime provinces- should confer with Sir Henry Thornton and his board of directors.
I trust that at the conference which is to be held, I believe, on the nineteenth of this month, there will be no directors absent, and I trust there will be no occasion for any director who may be absent to say that a policy has been determined upon at one meeting of the board and reversed at another. Such a thing was said and said openly by one of the directors, and when I ask a question in the House about it I am. told that it is not wise in the public interest to give information as to the private transactions of the board. The government in that respect is adoring idols that it burned, because it is not so long since prominent members of the party were declaiming against the previous government because it refused to bring before the House matters of -what might be called an internal nature. But I trust the government is going to stand by its policy in that regard. I do not ask them to reveal the details of every contract, but we do say that when an important resolution is taken which affects three provinces, the people of those provinces through their representatives in this House have a right to the information and have a right to get it here instead of going to some meeting place in Montreal or elsewhere, hat in hand, and asking Sir Henry Thornton to be good enough to lay aside his jests for a time and tell them of the inner working of the railway organization. Members should ask in the House and members should ght the information here.
Speaking from a New Brunswick standpoint-and I think I can include the Maritime provinces-I may say that there is dissatisfaction to-day. The people who voted there in the last election voted against my right hon. friend and leader because his declaration as to region apparently did not go far enough to please them; and they voted on the basis of what was being said on public platforms by representatives of the party that is now dominant. They trusted to those promises-that if the Liberal party were to come into power there would be a very decisive revolution in railway circles in the Maritime provinces. Prosperity would go on, employment would be ample, freight rates would be reduced and, above all, the management of an important section of the road was to be centralized at Moncton. The people unfortunately believed this. To-day the people see whether those statements were quite worthy of belief or not.
The absolutely sound, the absolutely sincere promises which were made by my right hon. leader were rejected by the people, and they took the illusory hallucinations projected from platform after platform by gentlemen who do not seem disposed to carry out one single particle of the obligations which they took during the campaign. What is the result today? That we have a railway and we have no national railway policy. Now, you cannot make a success out of an aggregation of rails, and fishplates and sleepers combined with rolling stock.
What I want to know-I am going to ask this House and I am not going to Sir Henry Thornton to ask it-is whether it is the policy of the government that this National road is to serve Canada or whether it is to serve a foreign country? I have asked in this House what the intention of this Railway Board is with regard to some proposed buildings in the vicinity of Providence, Rhode Island. I have not been able to get an answer, my question remains on the order paper. I had an intimation, through a fellow member, the other day that it was considered the answer might be embarrassing. That is not enough for me. I am entitled to know the whole of the details, and if there is a matter that is embarrassing I have a right to be told in confidence why it is embarrassing and to be allowed to use my judgment as to whether the explanation is sufficient or not.
In the Maritime provinces we are confronted, and have been confronted in the past, with a very distinct menace and that is the short route from Montreal to Portland, Maine, and the centralization of the activities of the Grand Trunk railway at that port. I want to know, the people of New Brunswick want to know, the people of the Maritime provinces want to know whether this road- the deficit on which is absolutely draining this country-is to be maintained by Canada, and by taxation upon the Dominion, in order to serve not only Portland, Maine, but Providence, Rhode Island, as well, and it is just about time that we had a clear and categorical answer to the question. We have not so far got it from the Board of Management, we have not got it in this House; all that we know is that there are newspaper items indicating a further expenditure of what is really the money of the people of Canada to carry this road a little farther into a foreign state. Is that a national policy? I cannot say the thing is going to be done because I cannot get an answer, the people of the Maritime provinces cannot get an answer, and the people of Canada are not getting an answer.

S upply-R ailways
I ask hon. members if that is a reasonable attitude for the government to assume in the transaction of public business?
I said that we want a national railway policy. I desire to emphasize that or rather to illustrate it. I can go back to confederation. I can refer to the building of the Intercolonial as a part of the contract of confederation-a road that most unfortunately was weighted down by what I would almost characterize as the stupidity of Downing street where, in their great fear of American invasion, they placed the road in a most difficult position from the standpoint of earning capacity. But placed as it was we got it. It has been of service to the Maritime provinces. For what purpose was it built? Surely to promote traffic between the Upper provinces, as they were then called, and the Maritime provinces. Now, I am not one of those who seeks to read into the bargain of confederation something that is not even plainly expressed in the contract. I do not say that the bargain of confederation contained any special provision by which the Maritime provinces were to have some wonderful rebate in rates, or some wonderful privileges that you cannot find in the written document. No doubt things of that character were said upon the public platform. On the other hand, I find in the compact of confederation. I find in the spirit of confederation, the idea of national unity-the idea that each part of the country would help each other part to bear the mutual burdens and to develop the interests of all as sympathetically and as fully as possible. Can we expect that from the Canadian National under the present policy or want of policy? If that policy is national all right. If that policy is international, then, in my judgment, it is all wrong.
I spoke of the attitude of the Maritime provinces towards Portland, Maine, with the possible addition of Providence, Rhode Island. What is the purpose of this road, considering the Intercolonial as part of it? Why, it simply reaches two points, Halifax and St. John, for the water borne commerce of the country during the period of the year when all the other Atlantic ports of Canada are sealed. If this road is national all the endeavours of its management will be directed towards carrying Canadian trade over that railway and through those ports. And I do not ask for supremacy for either one or the other; let them take their fair chance for the trade they can handle. But we do not find that being done. We get a hint of development-further development-in a foreign country. We have the actual proof by an answer to a question that I put in this House. We have the actual proof that where not one bushel of grain was shipped from 
Halifax, last year there were, I think, 17,000,000 bushels shipped to Portland, Maine. The system had been united then. Was there no possibility of any divergence of traffic to the Maritime provinces? Are we going to bs eternally told that the shippers routed that grain via that particular route? If I wen told that I would not believe it. If I were told that I would say " Has the Canadian National no agencies, no canvassers, no ability to see that traffic is diverted to our own ports in our own provinces?" Why, the traffic in grain of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is not under national control, from St. John practically equalled what the nation was doing through Portland, Maine. It is a nice admission to have to make that the uncontrolled private corporation was doing more for Canada than the incubus which is draining us year by year in taxation and through, I think, misdirection. We got about 2,000,000 bushels of grain through the government road in St. John, none in Halifax, while the bulk was going through the United States. That does not suit me, it does not suit the people of the Maritime provinces, and if the people of the Maritime provinces could drop their politics for five minutes this House would be electrified on that subject.
Now, can we have a national policy which will regard this road as tributary to the ocean ports, which will equip the ports as they need to be equipped, which will, if necessary, put on a differential rate against Portland, Maine, and against Providence, Rhode Island, so that the dream which was so beautifully voiced by that great Canadian, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, may at last be realized, that every pound of Canadian freight shall be carried on Canadian railways and exported through Canadian channels? I am broad enough in my politics to realize a good policy when I hear it enunciated, and the doctrine of Sir Wilfrid Laurier is good enough for me and for every man, woman and child in the Maritime provinces. What we want is action to carry it out, but I am not cheered, and the people of the Maritime provinces are not heartened, when we see items in the press that some other port in the United States is to be developed, and when we are confronted with ministerial silence if we ask a question about it.
There has been spme agitation in what I might call the local railway point in the Maritime provinces, the city of Moncton. This agitation has had regard to two things. One of them is what I referred to some time ago as the second deportation of the Acadians. It is not forgotten yet in that locality. I do not think-and I believe the Secretary of State (Mr. Copp) will agree with me-that it will be forgotten for a considerable

Supply-R ailways
time: that is the moving some of the people from one part of the road to another in connection with the audit business. It may have been necessary. I am not familiar enough with the railway business to know whether it was necessary or not. Naturally Moncton, like any other centre striving for population as it is, ambitious and rightly proud of its growing position in the Maritime provinces, does not like to see any lessening of its prestige or of its population. There may be a reason for that movement, but I fail to see it. I would think that the work could be done at Moncton, but I am not going to condemn the action in this regard in unmeasured terms, because I think there might possibly be an explanation. I will say, however, that the people of that locality are yet waiting for an explanation which has never yet been given by anybody, and until they get it they have a right to be dissatisfied.
Then we come to the major question-the question of control. The people have been given nominally the local control at Moncton of the road as it is being run to Montreal. We are told that at another meeting of the board that arrangement was changed, and now it is to be Riviere du Loup, or it may be some other way station on the road, but it makes very little difference where it is. I am not concerned with the particular amount of mileage within that region. It is not the trackage, it is not the number of locomotives, it is not anything of that kind that' counts. What we are concerned about in the Maritime provinces is where this board is placing the directing mind. Put a man at Moncton and tell him to take charge of that region, and while one railway man may not be quite as good as another, I have no doubt we can get a very capable man, whose orders will be obeyed by the subordinates, under whose direction trains will be moved regularly, freight will be moved promptly and public convenience will be met.
When we have got all that we have not touched the fringe of the real vital question of interest to the Maritime provinces. You have to put somebody in charge of that road, and you have to put him where he will be in direct contact with those in charge of the different regions, so that, instead of getting his information days too late to act upon it, he will be able to walk across the corridor and say to a man in charge af another region "What about such a class of freight? Why do you not arrange to send that freight through the ports of the Maritime provinces?" That is the vital thing. That is what we want, what we need and what we have a right to
if the policy is national instead of international.
I suppose someone will say I have made a plea for moving the headquarters to Montreal. I have done nothing of the kind, but I want to see some one in high authority in charge of operations. The ordinary business of the division or region, or whatever you may call it, can be managed from Moncton, but I want to know that there is somebody high in authority over that region, who will be sitting right at the nerve centre of the railway system, right in the city of Montreal or wherever it is to be, because upon the ability of the manager of that region to impress upon the managers of other regions that they should use all their activities to direct the freight originating in other parts of Canada down to the Maritime provinces, depends the success or the failure of the old Intercolonial railway, and upon that depends whether confederation is a mere dream or whether it shall be a vivid reality to the people of the present day living in those provinces.
I am not a secessionist. I do not think anything could make me a secessionist, but I say there are people and they are largely in the province from which the. Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) comes, as there are some in my own province, who are beginning to talk of getting out of confederation. We are coming to rather an unfortunate pass when, during this session, I hear from one part of the House an argument put forward that to get grain or goods out of the country by the shortest and cheapest route is the desideratum of a particular district, and that the rest of the country must be ignored, but I find, on going home and looking over the situation, that there is a very real, though I hope not very extensive, movement as yet, for getting out of the union which some people in the Maritime provinces feel is only a delusion to them. I think we come here to make conditions better instead of worse. I think we can help materially to make them better, if we can get a railway policy which the people will realize is intended to help them, to serve them, to develop and stimulate Canadian trade through Canadian territories, and which will, as quickly as possible, get rid of every avenue through the United States which diverts from Canada traffic that ought to be handled in Canada and handled by Canadian roads.
I will go a step further. There is on the statute book to-day, and there has been for many years a provision by which the British preference can be limited to goods arriving directly at a Canadian port. My sympathy is entirely with the British preference. I
Suppl y-Railways

think the sympathy of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has been with it for years;" he has expressed and has carried out that view. But I maintain that it is no harm to anyone who wants to import goods from England to be told: "You shall be allowed to import those goods under the terms of the British preference if you will just put them in a British bottom and bring them into a Canadian port. But if you want to tranship them through a foreign country, then you will have to pay the same rate of duty as you do on goods that do not have British origin." An order in council is all that is required to bring this state of affairs about. What would the benefit be? Just this, that where in the winter time we can send out from St. John or Halifax steamships well filled with cargoes, there is always a rather slender cargo coming in, and while I do not say that this would be great enough to revolutionize traffic entirely, it would be a very big and welcome step in the right direction. There would come through Halifax or St. John in the winter time thousands of tons of merchandise that do not come in through them now. The coming in of those hundreds of thousands of tons through ports of a foreign country is enabling freight rates on those steamships on other merchandise to be kept down in that foreign country for the benefit of the foreign ports. Whatever differences we may have on any possible political subject, there is one thing that I believe we agree upon in this chamber. I believe we are national in our aspirations; I do not believe there is anyone who wants to do anything that is not distinctly along the national line. I say therefore, believing that as I do, that this is an opportunity for a national policy which will reconcile the Maritime provinces, which have undoubtedly lost much through confederation, to the difficulties under which they have laboured, to the difficulties of present-day conditions, by feeling that they have, at least, the sympathy of the rest of Canada and that that sympathy is being translated into real action for the purpose of conferring upon them a real benefit. .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not rise for the purpose of answering my hon. friend, for I confess as a Maritime man I find myself so largely in sympathy with what he has been saying that I have no desire to break the force of it. But I think, in fairness, I ought to say that he has overlooked a very important point. Wq had for years two winter ports in Canada, Halifax and St. John. My hon. friend has very fairly said that they have fMr. Baxter.]
rivalries, and that they must be left to work those out as best they can. I concur in that. But my hon. friend has forgotten that by the action of the government of Canada in acquiring the Grand Trunk railway, we have acquired another Maritime port at Portland, Maine. The question is an ugly one, and this complicates it. We own the Grand Trunk railway, and Portland is the Grand Trunk railway terminus. This is the problem we are giving to Sir Henry Thornton. We are asking him to make these roads reasonably profitable, remunerative, self-sustaining. We give him this road to Portland. Is he to let that road be idle, to let the rails get rusty, or to try to send some traffic over the Portland road in order that it may contribute something towards the cost of the system- I am not discussing the merits of the Grand Trunk system ; but I am pointing to the fact that when we acquired the Grand Trunk railway system and opened a line to Portland, we were creating a rival to Halifax and St. John, and there is no use in ignoring the situation that confronts us to-day.
With nearly all that my hon. friend said historically and otherwise, I am entirely in sympathy. I know much of the feeling in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Many of the things I hear to-day are but an echo of the things I heard sixty years ago. The story is an old one to many of us whose hair is growing gray. I do not want to revive these matters "to-day. I sympathize with the desire of my hon. friend that we should look at all these things from the purely national viewpoint. I know that is his desire; I appreciate that, and I would like to co-operate with him. But let us not wink at the fact that since we have acquired the Grand Trunk with the road to Portland, we want that road to make some money, and we must, face the fact that we have deliberately set up a rival to St. John and Halifax.

If we have to let go practically the Grand Trunk from Montreal to Portland, if it does not pay, do- we not get the same traffic over our own road to our own ports? May I point this out to my hon. friend? To-day, the Intercolonial, everything from Montreal east, is losing money for want of traffic, so that the Grand Trunk may show a profit from Montreal to Portland. Let the latter be the losing end and let ours be the profitable end. The result will be that-and I say this with all pleasantness-instead of Yankee workmen and trainmen handling our products in the United States, good Canadians shall be handling them at Canadian ports

Supply-Rail ways
and through Canadian territory. If the loss must be on either one part of the system or the other, let the loss be to Portland.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would it not have been wise if we had considered that before we acquired that Yankee connection down at Portland?
I did not acquire it, and if it had to be acquired through any effort of mine, it would never have been acquired.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All right.

It is really refreshing to see how many twists and turns such an adept politician as the Minister u. Finance (Mr. Fielding) is, can give to any and every question. One minute we are told that this is an old, old story, sixty years old; it is getting hoary; it is getting gray with everybody who is gray-headed in the Maritime provinces, and they are feeling very sad about it. It is the same thing, the same chicken, the same trouble. There is no difference. We get that one minute, and the next we are told that the whole reason of this is because the late government bought the Grand Trunk railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that.
Perhaps my hon. friend would tell me what he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) was referring generally to the discontent in Nova Scotia as regards confederation, and I said that that was an old story we had heard all these sixty years ago. The reference to the railway is quite recent. His particular grievance is that we are sending business to Portland. My point was that the government of Canada made Portland one of our terminal points, and we have to face and recognize that fact.

Yes, we stand
just where we were. The talk was on this railway question; the talk was that this railway question to-day was inflaming the people who had troubles regarding confederation, and my hon. friend knows very well that for many years the Grand Trunk has been operating to Portland. Why, the trouble was just the same before. There is just this real difference that before the government owned the Grand Trunk, the government could not do anything: but through the Grand Trunk the government are now in a position to feed, if they want to feed. That is the only difference. My hon. friend says that the late government created Portland. We did not add one cent to Portland's facilities or anything else. I do not know whether my hon. friend i3 anticipating doing so. I see from the papers apparently his board is considering adding to the American facilities. It is quite true that if this question of ownership is to be made a reason by my hon. friend for multiplying American facilities and increasing American trade at the expense of Canadian trade, there is something in the suggestion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). These are aids they could not give if they did not own the line. But they are not compelled to do it; the action was their action. Certainly the acquisition of the Grand Trunk, instead of making it hard for the government to see that the Maritime provinces get their share of the business, makes it easy. Why, before they had no control whatever over that business; it was going Grand Trunk via Portland, to as great an extent as it is now going. They shipped everything down that way. This is no new story; it is something which did not commence with the acquisition of the Grand Trunk, and my hon. friends know that. They know that the Portland cry as against Halifax and St. John is an old cry, and yet my hoh. friend says that we created this situation when we bought the Grand Trunk. I think my hon. friend on further consideration will really do himself the justice in this House of acknowledging that the Grand Trunk sent all its business to Portland; he will acknowledge that all their grain was sent that way and that he himself in this very chamber in opposition, if my recollection is correct, pointed out the evils of that situation. If he did not, at any rate he vociferously applauded that position taken by gentlemen- from his own province when in opposition at that time. I do not see why it should be necessary to try to drag a political issue into a matter of this kind, particularly when it is so perfectly obvious that the business was sent through Portland before and when the only change made is that the government, if they so desire, are put just in a little better position than they ever were before to see to it that the Maritime provinces get whatever measure of justice they are entitled to. Before, they had not the power to do it; they have now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let the rails rust.

My hon. friend says, let the rails rust. Well, perhaps he will distribute the rust a little bit. Let the rails rust! I am not asking to let any rails rust. But does my hon. friend object more to letting the rails rust on the Grand Trunk Portland line than he objects to their rusting on the line to St. John? Why, to-day the Min-
Supply-Railways

ister of Railways is in a position in which he can control the traffic; he is in a position in which he can work up the traffic and see that it goes in this direction or that direction, through the large organization that is now right at his hand. Yet he says, let the rails rust. Well, I ask, is all the rust to be allowed to occur op the Canadian rails and none on the American? Or does not my hon. friend think that a little reciprocity there might be a good thing and that St. John might be allowed to have some of the business?
If I did not know something about this matter I might be impressed. But this is like a comedy.
I think it is.
Really it is a comedy. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance was running the Grand Trunk for quite a long time.
No.

Yes, it came under a board, with which he was connected, like the Canadian National Board. But that is not the question at all. The government bought a property, part of which is in the United States. Now, I was not a member of the House at the time but I did take occasion in two or three articles I had the privilege of writing to point out that difficulties might arise when the Canadian government became the owner of railway lines in the United States. Here is one of them presented to-day. It must not be forgotten that what is good at one end of the line is good at the other and the road to Portland is just as much the property of the people of Canada as is the road to Halifax. We have our money invested in it. But there is another feature of the matter, we must consider. Cut off the traffic going to the Grand Trunk from Chicago and vicinity, and there will be a lot that goes to Portland which will not go over the Grand Trunk at all. We cannot take the position of wanting to keep one end of the Grand Trunk in the United States and run it for our own benefit bringing traffic to Canadian ports, unless we are prepared to make a somewhat fair division and give some of the traffic that we get in Canada to the United States portion of the railway. The Grand Trank owned by the people of Canada runs for a portion of its length under the control of the various states of the United States and of the federal authority as well.
In the statistics that I referred to, it is Canadian wheat that is handled down there now.

Well, my hon. friend must remember that in the statistics given this year at the port of Montreal the charge was made that we were handling United States wheat to the detriment of facilities for handling Canadian wheat. We are living beside a great nation, and when we have launched into the experiment of owning railways, a portion of which is in the country beside us, we must be a little bit reciprocal in our arrangements or we shall find that they can ruin us more quickly that we can ruin them. Now, my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) in so far as his Canadian citizenship is concerned, is the owner of every foot of the line in the United States just as much as he is the owner of the system in Canada; and while it is better in so far as we can to have Canadian traffic handled at Canadian ports, we must bear in mind that the Canadian ports if they are to be made successful, must reciprocate and handle traffic from the United States and in order to do that we must be somewhat careful. I agree with my hon. friend that in so far as it is possible at all we ought to develop our own Canadian ports, but we must go about it in a manner that will not absolutely ruin our investment or reduce the efficiency of the railways to any great extent as a result of retaliatory measures from the United States. It makes no difference, particularly now, who bought the Grand Trunk. The fact is that we have it. The situation to which my hon. friend referred as to further development at Portland is one which I thought he thoroughly understood. But if it had been fully explained to him I think perhaps he would not ask the question he has asked. On some other occasion I shall be at liberty to discuss the matter fully; but when I tell him, who has been a member of a government, that certain conditions sometimes arise in which it is not in the public interest to answer certain questions, I think he will fully understand that the government cannot at all times give a " yes " or a " no " in reply to some direct questions when they believe that the answer might be detrimental to the whole interests of the country.
Now, the Canadian National system is not the system it was a few years ago. It was a difficult task that Mr. Hanna had when he had control of the Canadian Northern and its ramifications and when he was managing for years the Intercolonial railway. It is no new story that the Intercolonial Railway is being managed by the Canadian National Railways. What was called the Canadian National Railway Board has managed the Intercolonial for years past, and it is nothing new. The hon. gentleman's friends were cognizant of that, and

Supply-R ailways
if we are to have the whole Canadian National system it cannot be otherwise.
But great as the problem was at that time it is much greater at present, and my hon. friend has clearly pointed out the reason. Heretofore the Canadian people owned the Canadian Northern and the ramifications of that company as well as the Intercolonial, Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific. These railways were for the most part in the Dominion and the difficulty of handling them was not nearly so great as it is at the present time. We have added now all the lines of that great company, the Grand Trunk, which has its best feeder from the west and its chief port on the Atlantic in United States territory. This cannot be changed all in a moment, but I can assure my hon. friend that while the difficulty which confronts Sir Henry Thornton and his board is very great -greater than almost can be imagined from the outside-yet he has in mind to give the Canadian ports the advantage in every case wherever it is possible to do so. I cannot go any further than that. The time will come when I shall be able to make a few remarks to my hon. friend with reference to some of the things he has referred to which I know will be eminently satisfactory to him. But at the present time I must say again that it would not be in the interests of the Canadian people, it would not be in the interests of Canadian ports, if I were to undertake to answer in the manner that they are asked several questions concerning the extension of the line in the United States.

I think everybody will
sympathize with the minister in his desire to put the National Railways on a business basis. Notwithstanding the pessimism which was voiced in the House during the immigration debates-I think the minister deserves some credit for the fine statement which he delivered to the House the other night as to the year's showing of the Canadian National Railways.
Now, the case of the Maritime provinces was considered last session by the special committee of which the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) was chairman. It was contended that by agreement at confederation the Maritime provinces were promised special treatment in railway rates and service. If such a policy of fixing rates by localities is to be followed we might as well wind up the National Railways, because the question of rates is a question of operating costs, it is not a question of east and west, or north and south. Rates and service are determined by operating costs, and thdt is the only economic
factor which fixes railway rates. Last session we had the western representatives asking for preferential rates to the head of the lakes for their basic products, grain and so on. If the principle of preferential rates were once recognized, we might as well abolish the Railway Commission.

No one is discussing rates
to-day.

Parliament has interfered
every session with the question of rates until to-day the Railway Commission is not fulfilling its functions as a rate controlling board. The question of rates is an economic, a business, a commercial question that affects every business man in the country, and if the Railway Commission was left to fix railway rates it would be far better for all concerned.
In 1917 a royal commission was appointed to go into the question of railways and transportation in this country. That commission was composed of Mr. A. H. Smith, President of the New York Central Railway, Sir Henry Drayton, then Chairman of the Railway Commission, and Mr. W. M. Acworth, an eminent British railway engineer. What did Mr. Smith say about advancing loans and making extensions promiscuously without the consent of the Railway Commission? He said:
Amend the regulating policy so that the Railway Commission may have jurisdiction over all railroads in the matter of maximum and minimum rates, the issuance of securities, the building of new railways, or the extension of lines, and other matters properly within the scope of governmental supervision.
Has that recommendation been carried out? No. Neither has any of the recommendations made by the other members of that commission. Parliament has gone over the head of the Railway Commission, and only recently this House decided to continue construction of the Hudson Bay railway, although that undertaking has been condemned by this royal commission on the ground that it is impracticable and will never pay interest on the capital outlay. All this will be found set out at page 62 of the report. Now other extensions are coming up. The whole question of rates has been interfered with by the duplication of our railways. We have three transcontinental systems where one would have been sufficient for many years to come. The proper regulation of railways by the Railway Commission is ignored to-day. For all the use the commission now is or for all it has to do its members might as well go over to Luxor and accidentally enter the tomb and become embalmed with King Tutankhamen.
Supply-Railways
In reference to the Railway Commission having control of rates, would this affect the proposed importation of Alberta coal into Ontario?

If this parliament is going to interfere in the way it did last session with the rates on grain to the head of the lakes it might just as well go into the coal business too, because coal is a necessity as well as grain. What I contend is that parliament should not interfere with the functions of the Railway Commission in regulating freight rates, passing on loans, extensions and so on. The question of this loan should first be submitted to the Railway Commission to see if they recommend it. If you are going to give the National Railways a chance, do so, but to say that certain localities shall have preferential treatment is wrong in principle. You cannot have efficient administration of our national lines except under the Railway Act and by the Railway Commission.

I had proposed, Mr. Chairman, to speak on this subject, but I did not anticipate that the particular phase of it to which I wish to address myself would be introduced this afternoon. I presume this vote will not be passed to-day, and that I shall have an opportunity of speaking when the subject is again taken up?
This is merely an item for refunding. We have yet to take up the whole railway estimates. The discussion today is really a little premature.
That is quite true, but now that the House has the matter before it I submit it is a more favourable time to continue this phase of it rather than bring it up in a detached form in a week's time.

I entirely agree with the manner in which my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways-or the Minister of National Defence and Acting Minister of Railways-(Mr. Graham) approached the question. He is mot throwing the blame for the Grand Trunk business on the late government. I appreciate that there are difficulties in connection with the matter. I appreciate also that he says he is going to do the best he can, and I hope he will, in connection with Canadian business. Of course, he is in a position now to do it, but he would not have been if the Grand Trunk had not been taken over. The proposed extensions at Providence, Rhode Island, have been under consideration for some time. I remember looking

into the subject some years ago, and in what I am about to say my hon. friend will correct me if my recollection is wrong. My recollection is that the Grand Trunk spent some	$6,000,000 or $7,000,000 in
connection with that branch and the question was whether we could save that six or seven millions by making further commitments-some $5,000,000 more, I think. But the result of the information I then got was that having regard to traffic, having regard to business and general railway conditions, we would be simply losing another $5,000,000 if we spent it on that work. My hon. friend may have more up-to-date information on the subject. The state authorities were very anxious that the work should go on; they were going to extend the time for its completion in order that it might proceed. There was also some suggestion as to what they were prepared to do, if we went ahead with this thing, with a view to helping out what looked like an impossible situation from the investor's standpoint. I would like, the minister to inform the committee as to how matters stand now with respect to the Providence situation. If the work is to go on, how much will it cost, and what changes have taken place in the matter of traffic?

The situation is about as my hon. friend has described it. The Grand Trunk Railway, under the late Mr. Hays, expended some $7,000,000 over there, under a charter from two states. Hon. members will recall that there was some legal difficulty over the construction or the want of construction of that road.
